passage:
Monday: Yash typed 'anyone up for cricket Sunday?' into the group chat, looked at it, and deleted it. Last time he'd asked, only one person replied, two hours later. Easier not to ask.
Thursday: Aadhya caught him at the cycle stand. 'We're doing chai and a movie at my place Saturday. Coming?'
'Nah, I've got stuff,' Yash said. 'Honestly, I like being on my own now.' He rode off fast so she couldn't see his face.
Saturday: Yash lay on his bed with headphones on and no music playing. The group chat pinged: a photo of five friends squashed on Aadhya's sofa, popcorn everywhere. 'Missing you 😅' someone wrote.
He muted the chat, felt safe for a second, and then the room went very quiet.

qa.q: What did Yash type into the group chat on Monday before deleting it?
qa.a: He typed 'anyone up for cricket Sunday?'

qa.q: Why did Yash ride off fast after saying he liked being on his own?
qa.a: He didn't want Aadhya to see his face, which suggests the claim was covering hurt and a fear of being turned down again.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Yash at this stage?
qa.a: He could answer 'Missing you' with one honest line, or send the cricket message after all; one small reach-out keeps the door from closing.

qa.q: How might Aadhya read Yash's 'Nah, I've got stuff'?
qa.a: Aadhya may take it to mean Yash doesn't care about the group and might stop inviting him, even though she clearly wanted him there.

grounding: It shows a teenager who stops reaching out and turns down invitations, feeling safer for a moment while losing the chance to connect.

passage:
Joseph set down his coffee and looked at his niece, curled on the window seat with her phone face down.
'When I was fifteen, Anjali, we moved to Kottayam. The boys in my new class had their own jokes. I tried twice to join in. After that, I stopped trying. I ate lunch in the library and told your grandmother I preferred books. I even believed it, mostly.
One Sunday a boy called Mathew asked if I wanted to come fishing. I said no before he'd finished the sentence. He never asked again. Saying no first felt like armour. But armour is heavy, and nobody can reach you through it.
It took a cousin's wedding, where I had to talk to people all day, for me to remember I liked them.'
Anjali turned her phone over, then back again.

qa.q: Where did Joseph eat lunch after he stopped trying to join in?
qa.a: He ate lunch in the library.

qa.q: What does Joseph mean when he says saying no first felt like armour?
qa.a: He means refusing before anyone could reject him felt safe, even though it also shut out people like Mathew who wanted to include him.

qa.q: What turning point might Joseph's story offer Anjali now?
qa.a: It invites her to notice whether she is saying no first too, and to say yes to one small invitation before the habit hardens.

qa.q: How might Anjali be taking her uncle's story?
qa.a: Turning her phone over and back suggests she sees something of herself in it and is unsure whether to respond.

grounding: It shows, through an uncle's memory of being fifteen, how pulling back and claiming to prefer solitude protected him but also cost him friendships.

Karthik: nah. I'll pass

Chaitanya: it's Sunday bro
Karthik: honestly I just prefer being alone these days. less drama
Chaitanya: did something happen? since the trip you've been kind of gone
Karthik: nothing happened. I'm fine
Karthik: you guys have your group anyway
Chaitanya: you ARE the group
Karthik: ok. have fun 👍
Karthik put the phone face down and stared at the ceiling. He hadn't texted anyone first in three weeks, not since the school trip, when they'd made the room plan without him. It was easier this way. If he didn't ask, no one could say no.

qa.q: How long had Karthik not texted anyone first?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why does Karthik say he prefers being alone?
qa.a: He feels hurt and wary after being left out of the room plan, so pulling back protects him from more rejection.

qa.q: What small step could Karthik take?
qa.a: Say yes to one plan, or tell Chaitanya honestly that the room plan on the trip hurt, instead of saying he's fine.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel reading 'you guys have your group anyway'?
qa.a: Chaitanya likely feels confused and a little hurt, since in Chaitanya's eyes Karthik is part of the group.

grounding: A teen stops texting first and says he prefers being alone, protecting himself from rejection but closing off connection.

passage:
In their small town near Gaya, the evening cricket on the school ground was the one thing Akash never missed. Then, two weeks ago, he dropped an easy catch in the final and someone on the other team shouted, "Butterfingers!" Everyone laughed, even his own side.
Since then he had found reasons. Homework. A headache. Helping his father at the shop. When Aparna from next door knocked to walk to tuition together, as they had for years, he said he'd come later, and then didn't go.
"You've gone quiet," Aparna said on Thursday, leaning over the wall.
"I like being on my own now," he said. "People are tiring."
She shrugged and walked off alone. Akash watched her go, then lay on his cot listening to the distant shouts from the ground. It hurt less than being laughed at. It also felt a lot like being forgotten.

qa.q: What did someone shout when Akash dropped the catch?
qa.a: Butterfingers!

qa.q: What does 'It also felt a lot like being forgotten' reveal about Akash?
qa.a: He feels lonely and sad, realising that his protective withdrawal also cuts him off from friends.

qa.q: What could help Akash before the withdrawal deepens?
qa.a: Walking to tuition with Aparna once, or telling her the laughter hurt, so connection starts again gently.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel walking to tuition alone?
qa.a: Aparna likely feels puzzled and a bit rejected, missing a friend who has suddenly pulled away.

grounding: After being laughed at, a teen skips cricket and tuition and says he likes being alone, trading the risk of hurt for loneliness.

passage:
Wanjiru used to be the one who organised Friday football on the estate behind her school in Nairobi. Since March, when her best friend moved to Mombasa and the group chat seemed to carry on without her, she had stopped messaging first.
Valentina, the exchange student from Argentina, asked her to art club three times. Wanjiru said she was busy three times.
You don't have to be nice to me because I'm alone, she wanted to say. Instead she said, "I'm more of a lone person. I like my own company."
In truth, she ate lunch in the library so no one could see she had nobody to sit with. On Saturday she heard laughter from the football pitch and closed her window.
It felt safe. If she didn't join, no one could leave her out again. But the weekends were getting very long.

qa.q: Where does Wanjiru eat lunch?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: Why does Wanjiru close her window when she hears laughter?
qa.a: She feels lonely and afraid of being left out again, so shutting it out feels safer.

qa.q: What small step could Wanjiru try?
qa.a: Accept Valentina's next invitation to art club just once, instead of saying she's busy.

qa.q: What might Valentina feel after being turned down three times?
qa.a: Valentina may feel discouraged and unsure whether Wanjiru likes her, even as she keeps trying.

grounding: A teen who lost her best friend stops reaching out and claims to prefer being alone, which shields her from rejection but deepens loneliness.

passage: The school library was Lalit's favourite hiding place now. At break, Pallavi found him in the back row with a book he wasn't reading. "We're all going for the inter-house match after school. Coming?" Lalit didn't look up. "I've got stuff." It was the third time this month. Since the class trip, when nobody had saved him a seat on the bus, he had stopped messaging the group first. If they wanted him, they could ask. When they did ask, like now, he said no anyway, before they could change their minds. "You used to love these matches," Pallavi said. Lalit shrugged. "I like being alone. It's easier." Pallavi stood there a moment longer, then left. Lalit watched her go through the glass door, and something in his chest dropped. He turned a page, though he hadn't read it.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi find Lalit at break?
qa.a: She found him in the back row of the school library with a book he wasn't reading.

qa.q: Why does Lalit say no before the others can change their minds?
qa.a: Lalit is afraid of being rejected again after the bus trip, so refusing first feels safer even though it leaves him lonely.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Lalit or Pallavi here?
qa.a: Lalit could say yes once, even for a short while; Pallavi could keep inviting him and tell him plainly that she wants him there.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel walking away from the library?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel confused and a little hurt, wondering if Lalit is annoyed with her, since he used to love these matches.

grounding: Shows a teenager who stops reaching out, turns down invitations and says he likes being alone, protecting himself but losing the chance to connect.
